Let $m \ge 1$, $s\ge 3$ and $n\ge m+2$. Define 
\[
\enm{\cal{A}} (n,s,m) = \left\lbrace \mbox{integral $m$-dimensional } X\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^n \ | \   h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1)) =0 \right\rbrace. 
\]

definition.raw:
We introduce two numerical invariants: 
\[
d_{n,s,m} = \min \left\lbrace \deg(X) \ | \  X\in \enm{\cal{A}} (n,s,m) \right\rbrace, \mbox{ and }
\]  
\[
\alpha (n,s,m) = \max \left\lbrace h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s)) \ | \ X\in \enm{\cal{A}}(n,s,m) \right\rbrace. 
\] 

Hence $\alpha(n,s,m)$ is the maximal number, over the set $\enm{\cal{A}}(n,s,m)$, of the linearly independent hypersurfaces of degree $s$ vanishing on some $X\in \enm{\cal{A}}(n,s,m)$.

Then: item[(i)] If kappa (X)ne -infty, then h^0(enmcalO _X(s)) le 2+s^2d/2. item[(ii)] If kappa(X) = -infty, Xncong enmP^2 and X is enmP^1-bundle over a smooth curve pi: Xrightarrow D such that the rational fibers have degree one (i.e., X is a scroll), then h^0(enmcalO _X(s)) le 1 + (s^2+2s)d/2. item[(iii)] We have h^0(enmcalO _X(s)) le 1 + (s^2+3s)d/2 and equality holds if and only if d=k^2 for some k such that binomk+22ge n+1, Xcong enmP^2 and X is isomorphic to either the degree k Veronese embedding of enmP^2 or to an isomorphic linear projection of it. item[(iv)] Otherwise, if omega_X^otimes 2(3) is nef, then h^0(enmcalO _X(s)) le 1 + (s^2+frac32s)d/2.

Let nge 6 be even. Then h^0(enmcalI _X(2)) ge binomn+22 - 1 - 5d for all smooth connected and non-degenerate surfaces of degree d. Moreover, there exists a smooth and connected surface Xsubset enmP^n such that deg (X) =n^2/4, h^0(enmcalI _X(2)) =0, and Xcong enmP^2.

proof.raw:
Let 
\[
\delta =  \left\lceil \left(\binom{n+s-1}{n}-1\right)/(s-1)\right\rceil.
\]
We show that $d_{n,s} = \delta$. 

For any integer $d\ge n$, the set $H(d,0;n)$ of all smooth and non-degenerate degree $d$ rational curves $X\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^n$ has the structure of a smooth and integral algebraic variety, whose general point $X$ has {\it maximal rank}: hence $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(t)) =0$ for some $t\in \enm{\mathbb{N}}$ if and only if $d t+1\geq h^0(\enm{\cal{O}}_{\enm{\mathbb{P}}^n}(t))$, i.e., whenever it is possible for the restriction morphism to be injective; see \cite{hi, be3}. Thus a general $X\in H(d,0;n)$ satisfies
\[
h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1)) =0 \ \ \mbox{ if and only if } \ \ (s-1)d+1\ge \binom{n+s-1}{n}. 
\] 
This implies that $d_{n,s}\leq \delta$, as we have a (rational) integral curve of degree $\delta$. 

For the converse inequality, consider any integral curve $Y\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^n$ such that $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _Y(s-1)) =0$, and let $k = \deg (Y)$. Since $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _Y(s-1)) =0$, we have $h^0(\enm{\cal{O}} _Y(s-1)) \ge \binom{n+s-1}{n}$. Since $Y$ is an integral curve (of arbitrary arithmetic genus), elementary considerations give 
\[
h^0(L) \le \deg (L)+1,
\] 
for an arbitrary line bundle $L$ on $Y$. Thus 
\[
\deg(\enm{\cal{O}}_Y(s-1))+1 = (s-1)k+1 \ge h^0(\enm{\cal{O}}_Y(s-1))\geq \binom{n+s-1}{n}.
\]
Taking the minimum, the latter inequality implies $d_{n,s}\geq \delta$, which completes the proof.

Since $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1))=0$, Riemann-Roch shows that the statement is true if $h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(s-1)) =0$. Otherwise, assume $h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(s-1)) >0$. Since $h^0(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(s-1)) \ge \binom{n+s-1}{n}$, Clifford's theorem gives $(s-1)d_{n,s} \ge 2\binom{n+s-1}{n}-2$. By Proposition \ref{i1}, we have 
\[
(s-1)(d_{n,s} -1)+2 \le \binom{n+s-1}{n}.
\]
Altogether, they give $\binom{n+s-1}{n}\le s-1$, contradicting the assumption $s\ge 3$.

proof.raw:
Let $H\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^n$ be a linear subspace with $\dim H = n-m$. Take a linear subspace $E\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^n$ such that $\dim E =m-1$
and $E\cap H=\emptyset$. By \cite{hi, be2} (for the case $n=4$), \cite{be2} (for the case $n=5$) and \cite{be3} (for the case $n\ge 6$), there exists a smooth rational curve $Y\subset H$ such that 
\[
\deg (Y) =d_{n-m,s},\ \ h^0(H,\enm{\cal{I}} _{Y,H}(s-1)) =0,\ \mbox{and} \ \ h^0(H,\enm{\cal{I}} _{Y,H}(s)) = \binom{n+s-m}{n-m} -d_{n-m,s}.
\]

Let $W'$ be the cone with vertex $E$ and such a curve $Y\subset H$ as its base. Up to a projective transformation, the
projective variety depends only on $Y$, and not on the choice of a linear space $E$ such that $E\cap H = \emptyset$. 
Consider the setting described in Remark \ref{ccc0} with $e =d_{n-m,s}$. Note that $W'$ is projectively equivalent to the $(m+1)$-dimensional minimal degree variety $W$ featured in Remark \ref{ccc0}. Let $X\subset W'$ be an integral divisor such that $X\in |h+df|$, upon an identification $W\cong W'$. Since $d\geq (s-1)d_{n-m,s}+1$, by Remark \ref{ccc0}, $X$ is not contained in any hypersurface of degree $s-1$. 

If $X$ were a cone, either its vertex is contained in $E$ or is a point on $Y$. In the first case, upon identification with $W$, as in Remark \ref{ccc0}, let $X'=u^{*}X$ be the pullback of $X$ through $u$. The image of $h\cap u^{*}X$ under the morphism $u$ would be a codimension-one linear space in $u(h)\cong E$. However, this is impossible, as the degree of $u(h\cap X)$ is $d-d_{n-m,s}>1$. 
The second case is not possible either, because the pullback $X'$ would contain the divisor $h$. However, $X'$ is integral because $u$ is an isomorphism outside $h$, and $X'$ cannot coincide with $h$, as $X$ is a divisor of $W$.

proof.raw:
Fix a general $C\in |\enm{\cal{O}} _X(s)|$. By Bertini's theorem, $C$ is a smooth and connected curve of degree $sd$. By the genus formula, $C$ has genus 
\[
g = 1 + (s^2d + \omega _X\cdot \enm{\cal{O}} _X(s))/2. 
\]
Multiplying by the section $C$ yields the exact sequence 
\begin{equation}\label{eqma1}
0 \to \enm{\cal{O}} _X\to \enm{\cal{O}} _X(s)\to \enm{\cal{O}} _C(s)\to 0.
\end{equation}

Thus $h^0(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(s)) \le h^0(\enm{\cal{O}} _C(s)) +1$, where equality holds if $h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X)=0$. \\
If $s^2d = \deg (\enm{\cal{O}} _C(s)) \le 2g-2$, then this divisor on $C$ is special and Clifford's theorem \cite[pp. 107--108]{acgh} gives 
\[
h^0(\enm{\cal{O}} _C(s)) \le 1 +s^2d/2. 
\]
Whence $h^0(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(s))\le 2 +s^2d/2$.

From now on, assume $s^2d\ge 2g-1$ (or equivalently, $\enm{\cal{O}} _C(s)$ is non-special). Again, by the genus formula, one has 
\[
\omega _X \cdot \enm{\cal{O}} _X(1) <0.
\] 
Note that Riemann-Roch gives $h^0(\enm{\cal{O}} _C(s)) =s^2d +1-g = \frac{1}{2}(s^2d -s\omega _X\cdot \enm{\cal{O}} _X(1))$.

Before we proceed, recall that a line bundle $\mathcal L$ on a projective variety $X$ of dimension $\ge 2$ is said to be \emph{nef} if $\mathcal L \cdot C\ge 0$, for every algebraic curve $C\subset X$. 
\begin{quote}
{\it Claim.} If $\omega _X \cdot \enm{\cal{O}} _X(1) <0$, then $\kappa (X)=-\infty$. \\
{\it Proof of the Claim.} Assume on the contrary that $\kappa (X)\ge 0$. Let $X'$ be the minimal model of $X$ and $\varphi: X\to X'$ be the corresponding morphism. Since $\kappa (X') =\kappa (X)\ge 0$, $\omega _{X'}$ is nef. We have $\omega _X \cong \varphi^\ast\omega _{X'} +E$, where $E$ is an effective divisor and $E = 0$ if and only if $X$ is minimal. Since $\varphi^\ast\omega _{X'}$ is nef and $\enm{\cal{O}}_X(1)$ is effective, we derive 
\[
( \varphi^\ast \omega _{X'} +E)\cdot \enm{\cal{O}} _X(1)\ge 0,
\]
which is a contradiction. 
\end{quote}
The {\it Claim} shows that the Kodaira dimension of $X$ is $\kappa (X) = -\infty$, and statement (i) is proven. 

We recall the Kawamata Rationality Theorem in the case of smooth surfaces. Let $X$ be a smooth projective surface such that $\omega _X$ is {\it not} nef. For each ample line bundle $\enm{\cal{L}}$ on $X$, the {\it nef-value} $\tau$ of $\enm{\cal{L}}$ with respect to $\omega_X$ is defined as 
\[
\tau(\enm{\cal{L}}) = \sup \lbrace t>0 \ | \  \enm{\cal{L}} +t\omega _X \mbox{ is nef} \rbrace, 
\]
where  $\enm{\cal{L}} +t\omega _X$ is viewed as a functional on the cone of curves depending on a parameter $t$. The aforementioned theorem states that the real number $\tau$ is rational, $\tau = u/v$, where $u$ is a positive integer and $v\in \{1,2,3\}$; see, e.g., \cite[Theorem 1.5.2]{bs}, \cite[Corollary 1-2-15]{matsuki}. Moreover, $\enm{\cal{L}} +\tau \omega_X$ is nef \cite[Lemma 1.5.5]{bs}, \cite[Theorem 1-2-14]{matsuki}. Thus
we have the following cases:

\begin{itemize}
\item $u=1$ and $v=3$. The cone of curves of $X$ has an {\it extremal ray} of {\it length} $3 =\dim X +1$; see \cite{matsuki} for these notions. This implies $X\cong \enm{\mathbb{P}}^2$ and $\enm{\cal{O}} _X(1)$ is the generator of $\mathrm{Pic}(X)$. Since $n\ge 4$, $X$ is embedded as described in the statement. 
\vspace{2mm}
\item $u=1$ and $v=2$. Since $\enm{\cal{L}}+\frac{1}{2}\omega _X$ is nef, so is the line bundle $2\enm{\cal{L}}+\omega _X$. In this case, there exists a curve $C\subset X$ such that $C\cdot (2\enm{\cal{L}}+\omega _X) =0$. By \cite[Theorem 1-4-8]{matsuki}, $X$ is a $\enm{\mathbb{P}}^1$-bundle over a smooth curve $D$, $\pi: X\to D$, and $\enm{\cal{L}}\cong\enm{\cal{O}} _X(1)$ has degree $1$ on each fiber $C$ of $\pi$. In such a case, $\omega _X(2)$ is nef and hence $\omega_X\cdot \enm{\cal{O}}_X(1) \geq -2$. This proves statement (ii). \\
\vspace{2mm}
\item $u\ge 2$ or $v=1$. Then $\omega _X^{\otimes 2}(3)$ is nef and therefore $\omega_X\cdot \enm{\cal{O}}_X(1)\geq -3/2$. In this case,
we obtain (iv). 
\end{itemize}
In conclusion, the discussion above yields $\omega_X\cdot \enm{\cal{O}}_X(1)\geq -3$ for all $X$, with equality if and only if $X\cong \enm{\mathbb{P}}^2$. This proves statement (iii).

proof.raw:
Let $H\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^n$ be a general hyperplane. Consider the exact sequence
\begin{equation}\label{eqw1}
0 \longrightarrow \enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1)\longrightarrow \enm{\cal{I}} _X(s)\longrightarrow \enm{\cal{I}} _{X\cap H,H}(s)\longrightarrow 0.
\end{equation}
Since $H$ is general, $C = X\cap H$ is a smooth curve of degree $d$ and genus $g$. Hence, by Riemann-Roch, $h^0(\enm{\cal{O}}_C(2)) \geq 2d+1-g$. 
Thus 
\[
h^0(H,\enm{\cal{I}} _{X\cap H,H}(2)) \le \binom{n+1}{2} - 2d-1+g.
\] 
By (\ref{eqw1}) and $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(1)) =0$, the conclusion follows.

remark.raw:
\label{i3}
Fix an integer $g$ such that $0\le g \le  (s-1)d_{n,s}+1-\binom{n+s-1}{n}$. Again, as in the proof of Lemma \ref{i2}, Proposition \ref{i1} yields
\[
(s-1)(d_{n,s} -1)+2 \le \binom{n+s-1}{n},
\] 
and so $g\le s-2$. 
\vspace{3mm}

\begin{quote}
{\it Claim.} We have $s-2 \le d_{n,s}-n$.\\
{\it Proof of the Claim.} By contradiction, assume $d_{n,s} \le n+s-3$. By Proposition \ref{i1}, in order to obtain a contradiction, it is enough to show 
\[
(s-1)(n+s-3) +2 \le \binom{n+s-1}{n}.
\] 
Let $\varphi (n,s) = \binom{n+s-1}{n} - (s-1)(n+s-3)-2$. This function is non-negative in the desired range. Indeed, consider
\[
\varphi (3,s) = (s+2)(s+1)s/6 -s(s-1)-2.
\]
It is clear this is non-negative for all $s\ge 3$. Moreover: 
\[
\varphi (n+1,s) -\varphi (n,s) =\binom{n+s-2}{n} -s+1 \ge 0, \ \ \mbox{ for all } \ \  s\ge 3, 
\]
which leads to a contradiction. 
\end{quote}

By the {\it Claim} and \cite{be2, be3}, a general curve $X\in H(d_{n,s},g;n)'$ has maximal rank. Moreover, for each integer $g$ with $0\le
g\le  (s-1)d_{n,s}+1-\binom{n+s-1}{n}$, there exists a curve $X\in H(d_{n,s},g;n)$ such that $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1))=0$. Since $h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(1)) =0$, we
have $h^0(\omega_X(-1)) = 0$. The latter condition is equivalent to $h^0(\omega_X(-t))=0$ for all $t\geq 1$. 
Hence $h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(t)) =0$ for $t=s-1,s$. Moreover, we have: 
\[
h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1)) = (s-1)d_{n,s}+1-g -\binom{n+s-1}{n},
\]
\[
h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s)) = h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s)) +\binom{n+s}{n} -sd_{n,s}-1+g.
\] 
Now, choose $g_0 = (s-1)d_{n,s} + 1 -\binom{n+s-1}{n}$, so that $h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1)) =0$. 
Furthermore 
\[
h^2(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-2)) =h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(s-2)) =0,
\] 
where the right-most equality holds because $s\ge3$. By the well-known Castelnuovo-Mumford's Lemma, we derive 
\[h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(t)) =0 \mbox{ for all } t\ge s. \] 
Finally,
\[
h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s)) =\binom{n+s}{n} -sd_{n,s}-1+g_0 = \binom{n+s-1}{n-1}-d_{n,s}.
\]

remark.raw:
\label{qw00}
In the setting of Lemma \ref{i00+}, as usual let $d = \deg (X)$ and $g = p_a(X)$. 
Since $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1)) =0$, by Riemann-Roch, we have 
\[
h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1)) = (s-1)d +1-g-\binom{n+s-1}{n}.
\] 
Define the numerical function $\psi (t) := h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(t-1)) -h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(t))$. For fixed integers $g$, $h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s))$ and $\psi(s)$, the right-hand side of (\ref{eqi00+}) is a strictly decreasing function in $d$.

Since $\deg (\enm{\cal{O}} _X(t)) =d+\deg (\enm{\cal{O}} _X(t-1))$, Serre duality and Riemann-Roch give 
\[
0\le \psi (t) \le d.
\]
Therefore a class of curves for which the term $h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(s-1)) -h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(s))$ is zero is realized when $h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(s-1)) =0$.

Moreover, note that the long exact sequence in cohomology of (\ref{eqi01}) yields
\[
h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s)) \le \binom{n+s-1}{n-1} -d,
\] 
whenever $h^1(H,\enm{\cal{I}} _{X\cap H,H}(s)) =0$. As in \cite[Chapter 3]{szp}, let $\chi$ denote the minimal non-negative integer such that $h^1(H,\enm{\cal{I}} _{X\cap H,H}(\chi +1)) =0$. As classically shown by Castelnuovo, using (\ref{eqi01}) one obtains $h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(t)) =0$ for all $t\ge \chi$ \cite[Theorem 1, p. 52]{szp}.
Furthermore, $h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(t)) \ge h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(t+1))$ for all $t\ge \chi$ \cite[Lemma 2, p. 53]{szp}, 
and $h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(t))> h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(t+1))$ whenever $t>\chi$ and $h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(t))\ne 0$.

remark.raw:
\label{x2}
Recall that, by Proposition \ref{i1}, 
\[
d_{3,s} = \left\lceil \left(\binom{s+2}{3}-1\right)/(s-1)\right\rceil.
\]  
For $d, s\ge 3$, to  each pair $(d,s)$, we attach the set of degree $d$ curves in $\enm{\mathbb{P}}^3$ 
{\it not} contained in any surface of degree $<s$. Given $(d,s)$, Halphen's question asks in particular to determine the maximum genus of a curve associated to this pair. It is customary to divide the set of pairs $(d,s)$ into four regions: \\

{\bf Range $\emptyset$}: $d < (s^2+4s+6)/6 $. In this range, there is no integral and non-degenerate curve $X\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^3$ such that
$\deg (X)=d$ and $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1))=0$ \cite[Theorem 3.3]{h0}, \cite{hh}. 

\vspace{5mm}
{\bf Range A}: $(s^2+4s+6)/6 \le d < (s^2+4s+6)/3$. In this range, one finds curves with  
$h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(s-1)) =0$ and hence $h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(s))=0$. Thus if $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1))=0$ and $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s)) \ne 0$, by Riemann-Roch one has $(s-1)d+1-g
\ge \binom{s+2}{3}$ and $sd+1-g\le \binom{s+3}{3}$. Moreover, if $\lceil s(s+2)/4\rceil \le d <(s^2+4s+6)/3$, it is known such a curve exists for any such choice of $(d,s)$, along with curves reaching the maximal genera allowed; see, e.g., \cite{bbem, fl1,fl2}.  To fill in all 
$(d,s)$ such that $(s^2+4s+6)/6\le d < \lceil s(s+2)/4\rceil$ the same result (the existence of curves with $(d,s)$ and $g= (s-1)d+1- \binom{s+2}{3}$) is only known for $s$ large enough, i.e., $s \geq 10.5\times 10^5$, by the recent \cite[Theorem 1]{be6}. 

\vspace{5mm}
{\bf Range B}: $(s^2+4s+6)/3\le d < s(s-1)$. Hartshorne and Hirschowitz constructed, for any $(d, s)$ in this range, smooth space curves with very high genera and conjectured that they have the maximal genus for all curves associated to $(d,s)$ \cite{hh, ms}. 

\vspace{5mm}
{\bf Range C}: $d>s(s-1)$. One finds a smooth degree $d$ space curve $X$ such that
$\deg (X)=d$ and $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1))=0$; Gruson and Peskine classified all such curves $X$ of maximal genus \cite{gp1}: 
if $d\equiv 0\pmod{s}$, these curves are complete intersections of a surface of degree $s$ and a surface of degree $d/s$; in all other
cases $X$ is {\it linked} to a plane curve $C$ of degree $\deg(C) = s\lceil d/s\rceil -d$, by the complete intersection of a surface of degree $s$
and a surface of degree $\lceil d/s\rceil$. For $d\geq s^2$, we have $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s)) \le 2$ with equality if and only if $d=s^2$
and $X$ is the complete intersection of two surfaces of degree $s$.

curves $X\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^n$ such that $h^i(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1)) =0$ for all $i\ge 0$; this is because for any curve $Y\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^n$, one has

\label{numrangexq1true}
Fix integers $n, d, g, s$ such that $n\ge 3$, $s\ge 3$, with 
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] $0 \le g \le d-n$, 

\item[(ii)] $(n+1)d \ge ng +n(n+1)$,

\item[(iii)] $(s-1)d \ge \binom{n+s-1}{n} +g-1$, and

\item[(iv)] $sd \le \binom{n+s-1}{n}+g-2$.
\end{enumerate}
By results shown in \cite{be2, be4, be5}, there exists a smooth, connected, and non-degenerate {\it maximal rank} 
curve $X\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^n$ with $\deg (X) = d$, arithmetic genus $p_a(X)=g$, and $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s)) =\binom{n+s}{n} -sd+g-1$. Hence, setting the arithmetic genus to be the maximal in this range, i.e., $g=d-n$, (i) and (ii) in Question \ref{xq1} have a positive answer, whenever
\[
h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s))>0 \Longleftrightarrow (s-1)d < \binom{n+s}{n} -n-1.
\]
Note that inequality (iii) implies $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1)) = 0$, because $X$ has maximal rank.

The map $\pi$ makes $T$ a $\enm{\mathbb{P}}^{m}$-bundle and hence $\mathrm{Pic}(T) \cong \enm{\mathbb{Z}}^2$, with basis given by a fiber $f$ of $\pi$ and any line bundle

_{\enm{\mathbb{P}}^1}(-e)^{\oplus m} \to \enm{\cal{O}} _{\enm{\mathbb{P}}^1}$, \cite[Ch. II]{h}). As an abstract variety,

Similarly to the case of surfaces \cite[Ch. V]{h}, for any $a, b\in\enm{\mathbb{Z}}$ we have $|ah+bf|\ne\emptyset$ if and only if either $a=0$ and $b\ge 0$ or $a>0$ and $b\ge ae$. The line bundle $\enm{\cal{O}}_T(ah+bf)$ is globally generated (resp. ample) if and only if $a\ge 0$ and $b\ge ae$ (resp. $a>0$ and $b>ae$). 

The complete linear system $h+ef$ induces a morphism $u: T\to \enm{\mathbb{P}}^n$, where $n =  e+m$, as $h^0(\enm{\cal{O}} _{\enm{\mathbb{P}}^1}(e)\oplus \enm{\cal{O}} _{\enm{\mathbb{P}}^1}^{\oplus m}) 
=e+1+m$. Let $W= u(T)$ be the image of $T$. The morphism $u$ contracts $h$ to an $(m-1)$-dimensional linear space in $\enm{\mathbb{P}}^r$, whereas $u|_{T\setminus h}$ is an
embedding. Thus $u$ is a morphism birational onto its image, as the support of $h$ is codimension-one. \\

\begin{quote}

{\it Proof of the Claim.} Since $u$ is a morphism birational onto its image, $\deg (W)= (h+ef)^{m+1}$, where the latter
integer is the intersection product in the Chow ring of $T$ of $m+1$ copies of the divisor $h+ef$ defining the morphism. 
Since any two different fibers of $\pi$ are disjoint, the class $f^2$ in the Chow ring is zero. Thus $(h+ef)^{m+1} = h^{m+1} +(m+1)eh^mf$.
Fix a fiber $F\in |f|$ of $\pi$. Since $h_{|F}$ is the degree one line bundle on $F$ and $F\cong \enm{\mathbb{P}}^{m}$, we have $h^{m}f =1$ and
hence $(m+1)eh^{m}f =(m+1)e$. \\
If $m=1$, $T$ is a rational ruled surface. The normal bundle of $h$ has degree $h^2=-e$. Hence the conclusion follows for $m=1$. \\
Assume $m\ge 2$. Since $h \cong \enm{\mathbb{P}}^1\times \enm{\mathbb{P}}^{m-1}$, we have
$\mathrm{Pic}(h)\cong \enm{\mathbb{Z}}^2$. As generators of the lattice $\mathrm{Pic}(h)$, we take the pullbacks of hyperplane classes of the factors through the projections $\pi _1: h\to \enm{\mathbb{P}}^1$ and $\pi _2: h\to \enm{\mathbb{P}}^{m-1}$, i.e., $\enm{\cal{O}} _h(1,0) = \pi _1^\ast (\enm{\cal{O}}_{\enm{\mathbb{P}}^1}(1))$ and $\enm{\cal{O}} _h(0,1) = \pi _2^\ast (\enm{\cal{O}} _{\enm{\mathbb{P}}^{m-1}}(1))$. \\

\begin{proof}
Let 
\[
\delta =  \left\lceil \left(\binom{n+s-1}{n}-1\right)/(s-1)\right\rceil.
\]
We show that $d_{n,s} = \delta$. 

For any integer $d\ge n$, the set $H(d,0;n)$ of all smooth and non-degenerate degree $d$ rational curves $X\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^n$ has the structure of a smooth and integral algebraic variety, whose general point $X$ has {\it maximal rank}: hence $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(t)) =0$ for some $t\in \enm{\mathbb{N}}$ if and only if $d t+1\geq h^0(\enm{\cal{O}}_{\enm{\mathbb{P}}^n}(t))$, i.e., whenever it is possible for the restriction morphism to be injective; see \cite{hi, be3}. Thus a general $X\in H(d,0;n)$ satisfies
\[
h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1)) =0 \ \ \mbox{ if and only if } \ \ (s-1)d+1\ge \binom{n+s-1}{n}. 
\] 
This implies that $d_{n,s}\leq \delta$, as we have a (rational) integral curve of degree $\delta$. 

For the converse inequality, consider any integral curve $Y\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^n$ such that $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _Y(s-1)) =0$, and let $k = \deg (Y)$. Since $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _Y(s-1)) =0$, we have $h^0(\enm{\cal{O}} _Y(s-1)) \ge \binom{n+s-1}{n}$. Since $Y$ is an integral curve (of arbitrary arithmetic genus), elementary considerations give 
\[
h^0(L) \le \deg (L)+1,
\] 
for an arbitrary line bundle $L$ on $Y$. Thus 
\[
\deg(\enm{\cal{O}}_Y(s-1))+1 = (s-1)k+1 \ge h^0(\enm{\cal{O}}_Y(s-1))\geq \binom{n+s-1}{n}.
\]
Taking the minimum, the latter inequality implies $d_{n,s}\geq \delta$, which completes the proof. 
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}
Since $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1))=0$, Riemann-Roch shows that the statement is true if $h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(s-1)) =0$. Otherwise, assume $h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(s-1)) >0$. Since $h^0(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(s-1)) \ge \binom{n+s-1}{n}$, Clifford's theorem gives $(s-1)d_{n,s} \ge 2\binom{n+s-1}{n}-2$. By Proposition \ref{i1}, we have 
\[
(s-1)(d_{n,s} -1)+2 \le \binom{n+s-1}{n}.
\]
Altogether, they give $\binom{n+s-1}{n}\le s-1$, contradicting the assumption $s\ge 3$.  
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}\label{i3}
Fix an integer $g$ such that $0\le g \le  (s-1)d_{n,s}+1-\binom{n+s-1}{n}$. Again, as in the proof of Lemma \ref{i2}, Proposition \ref{i1} yields
\[
(s-1)(d_{n,s} -1)+2 \le \binom{n+s-1}{n},
\] 
and so $g\le s-2$. 
\vspace{3mm}

\begin{quote}
{\it Claim.} We have $s-2 \le d_{n,s}-n$.\\
{\it Proof of the Claim.} By contradiction, assume $d_{n,s} \le n+s-3$. By Proposition \ref{i1}, in order to obtain a contradiction, it is enough to show 
\[
(s-1)(n+s-3) +2 \le \binom{n+s-1}{n}.
\] 
Let $\varphi (n,s) = \binom{n+s-1}{n} - (s-1)(n+s-3)-2$. This function is non-negative in the desired range. Indeed, consider
\[
\varphi (3,s) = (s+2)(s+1)s/6 -s(s-1)-2.
\]
It is clear this is non-negative for all $s\ge 3$. Moreover: 
\[
\varphi (n+1,s) -\varphi (n,s) =\binom{n+s-2}{n} -s+1 \ge 0, \ \ \mbox{ for all } \ \  s\ge 3, 
\]
which leads to a contradiction. 
\end{quote}

By the {\it Claim} and \cite{be2, be3}, a general curve $X\in H(d_{n,s},g;n)'$ has maximal rank. Moreover, for each integer $g$ with $0\le
g\le  (s-1)d_{n,s}+1-\binom{n+s-1}{n}$, there exists a curve $X\in H(d_{n,s},g;n)$ such that $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1))=0$. Since $h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(1)) =0$, we
have $h^0(\omega_X(-1)) = 0$. The latter condition is equivalent to $h^0(\omega_X(-t))=0$ for all $t\geq 1$. 
Hence $h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(t)) =0$ for $t=s-1,s$. Moreover, we have: 
\[
h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1)) = (s-1)d_{n,s}+1-g -\binom{n+s-1}{n},
\]
\[
h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s)) = h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s)) +\binom{n+s}{n} -sd_{n,s}-1+g.
\] 
Now, choose $g_0 = (s-1)d_{n,s} + 1 -\binom{n+s-1}{n}$, so that $h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1)) =0$. 
Furthermore 
\[
h^2(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-2)) =h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(s-2)) =0,
\] 
where the right-most equality holds because $s\ge3$. By the well-known Castelnuovo-Mumford's Lemma, we derive 
\[h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(t)) =0 \mbox{ for all } t\ge s. \] 
Finally,
\[
h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s)) =\binom{n+s}{n} -sd_{n,s}-1+g_0 = \binom{n+s-1}{n-1}-d_{n,s}.
\]
\end{remark}

To summarize, in Remark \ref{i3}, we have shown the following: 

\begin{remark}\label{observation}
Setting $g_0 = (s-1)d_{n,s} + 1 -\binom{n+s-1}{n}$, We have: 
\[
d_{n,s} \ge n+g_0;
\]
additionally, a general curve $X\in H(d,g_0;n)'$ satisfies 
\[
h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1)) =0 \mbox{ and } h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s))=\binom{n+s-1}{n-1} -d_{n,s}.
\]
\end{remark}


\begin{question}\label{qw0}
Is it true that 
\[
\alpha (n,s) = \binom{n+s-1}{n-1} -d_{n,s}?
\] 
Keep the definition of $g_0$ from Remark \ref{observation}. Does equality hold if and only if $X$ is a general curve in $H(d_{n,s}, g_0; n)'$?
\end{question}

\begin{proof}
Fix a general hyperplane $H\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^n$. Note that $h^0(H,\enm{\cal{I}} _{X\cap H}(s)) =\binom{n+s-1}{n-1}-\deg (X)+h^1(H,\enm{\cal{I}} _{X\cap H}(s))$. Since $h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(t)) =h^2(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(t))$ for all $t\in \mathbb Z$, in order to conclude it is sufficient to use the long exact sequence in cohomology of the exact sequence
\begin{equation}\label{eqi01}
0\to \enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1)\to \enm{\cal{I}} _X(s)\to \enm{\cal{I}} _{X\cap H,H}(s)\to 0, 
\end{equation}
along with the assumption $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1)) =0$.
\end{proof}

Now we discuss the term appearing on the right-hand side of equality (\ref{eqi00+}). 

\begin{remark}\label{qw00}
In the setting of Lemma \ref{i00+}, as usual let $d = \deg (X)$ and $g = p_a(X)$. 
Since $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1)) =0$, by Riemann-Roch, we have 
\[
h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1)) = (s-1)d +1-g-\binom{n+s-1}{n}.
\] 
Define the numerical function $\psi (t) := h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(t-1)) -h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(t))$. For fixed integers $g$, $h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s))$ and $\psi(s)$, the right-hand side of (\ref{eqi00+}) is a strictly decreasing function in $d$.

Since $\deg (\enm{\cal{O}} _X(t)) =d+\deg (\enm{\cal{O}} _X(t-1))$, Serre duality and Riemann-Roch give 
\[
0\le \psi (t) \le d.
\]
Therefore a class of curves for which the term $h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(s-1)) -h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(s))$ is zero is realized when $h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(s-1)) =0$.

Moreover, note that the long exact sequence in cohomology of (\ref{eqi01}) yields
\[
h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s)) \le \binom{n+s-1}{n-1} -d,
\] 
whenever $h^1(H,\enm{\cal{I}} _{X\cap H,H}(s)) =0$. As in \cite[Chapter 3]{szp}, let $\chi$ denote the minimal non-negative integer such that $h^1(H,\enm{\cal{I}} _{X\cap H,H}(\chi +1)) =0$. As classically shown by Castelnuovo, using (\ref{eqi01}) one obtains $h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(t)) =0$ for all $t\ge \chi$ \cite[Theorem 1, p. 52]{szp}.
Furthermore, $h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(t)) \ge h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(t+1))$ for all $t\ge \chi$ \cite[Lemma 2, p. 53]{szp}, 
and $h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(t))> h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(t+1))$ whenever $t>\chi$ and $h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(t))\ne 0$.


\end{remark}

Note that the proof of Proposition \ref{i1} shows that a curve in $\mathcal A(n,s)$ of minimal degree $d_{n,s}$ can be chosen to be smooth (and rational). 
More generally, we wonder the following: 

\begin{question}\label{xq1}
Let $n\ge 3$, $s\ge 3$ and $d> d_{n,s}$. 
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] Is there an integral and non-degenerate curve $X\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^n$ such that $\deg (X)=d$, $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1)) =0$ and
$h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s))\ne 0$?
\item[(ii)] Can we choose such an $X$ to be smooth?
\end{enumerate}
\end{question}

In the next two remarks we recall our knowledge around Question \ref{xq1} for $n=3$. 

\begin{remark}\label{x2}
Recall that, by Proposition \ref{i1}, 
\[
d_{3,s} = \left\lceil \left(\binom{s+2}{3}-1\right)/(s-1)\right\rceil.
\]  
For $d, s\ge 3$, to  each pair $(d,s)$, we attach the set of degree $d$ curves in $\enm{\mathbb{P}}^3$ 
{\it not} contained in any surface of degree $<s$. Given $(d,s)$, Halphen's question asks in particular to determine the maximum genus of a curve associated to this pair. It is customary to divide the set of pairs $(d,s)$ into four regions: \\

{\bf Range $\emptyset$}: $d < (s^2+4s+6)/6 $. In this range, there is no integral and non-degenerate curve $X\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^3$ such that
$\deg (X)=d$ and $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1))=0$ \cite[Theorem 3.3]{h0}, \cite{hh}. 

\vspace{5mm}
{\bf Range A}: $(s^2+4s+6)/6 \le d < (s^2+4s+6)/3$. In this range, one finds curves with  
$h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(s-1)) =0$ and hence $h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(s))=0$. Thus if $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1))=0$ and $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s)) \ne 0$, by Riemann-Roch one has $(s-1)d+1-g
\ge \binom{s+2}{3}$ and $sd+1-g\le \binom{s+3}{3}$. Moreover, if $\lceil s(s+2)/4\rceil \le d <(s^2+4s+6)/3$, it is known such a curve exists for any such choice of $(d,s)$, along with curves reaching the maximal genera allowed; see, e.g., \cite{bbem, fl1,fl2}.  To fill in all 
$(d,s)$ such that $(s^2+4s+6)/6\le d < \lceil s(s+2)/4\rceil$ the same result (the existence of curves with $(d,s)$ and $g= (s-1)d+1- \binom{s+2}{3}$) is only known for $s$ large enough, i.e., $s \geq 10.5\times 10^5$, by the recent \cite[Theorem 1]{be6}. 

\vspace{5mm}
{\bf Range B}: $(s^2+4s+6)/3\le d < s(s-1)$. Hartshorne and Hirschowitz constructed, for any $(d, s)$ in this range, smooth space curves with very high genera and conjectured that they have the maximal genus for all curves associated to $(d,s)$ \cite{hh, ms}. 

\vspace{5mm}
{\bf Range C}: $d>s(s-1)$. One finds a smooth degree $d$ space curve $X$ such that
$\deg (X)=d$ and $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1))=0$; Gruson and Peskine classified all such curves $X$ of maximal genus \cite{gp1}: 
if $d\equiv 0\pmod{s}$, these curves are complete intersections of a surface of degree $s$ and a surface of degree $d/s$; in all other
cases $X$ is {\it linked} to a plane curve $C$ of degree $\deg(C) = s\lceil d/s\rceil -d$, by the complete intersection of a surface of degree $s$
and a surface of degree $\lceil d/s\rceil$. For $d\geq s^2$, we have $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s)) \le 2$ with equality if and only if $d=s^2$
and $X$ is the complete intersection of two surfaces of degree $s$.
\end{remark}


\begin{remark}\label{x3}
Assume $(d,s)$ is in {\bf Range A}. Let
$X\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^3$ be any integral curve with $\deg (X)=d$, $h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(s-1)) =0$, $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1)) =0$, and $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s))

We generalize {\bf Range A} to curves embedded in $\enm{\mathbb{P}}^n$ for any $n\geq 3$. For all integers $n\geq 3$, $s\ge 2$ and $d\ge d_{n,s}$, let $\enm{\cal{B}} (n,s,d)$ (resp. $\enm{\cal{B}} (n,s,d)'$) denote the set of all smooth and connected (resp. integral) $X\in \enm{\cal{A}} (n,s)$ such that $\deg (X)=d$ and $h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(s-1)) = 0$.

\begin{definition}
Curves in $\enm{\cal{B}} (n,s,d)$ are said to be in the {\it generalized} {\bf Range A}.
\end{definition}

\begin{remark}
Let $X\in \enm{\cal{B}} (n,s,d)'$. Since $h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(s-1))  =0$, 
Riemann-Roch gives $h^0(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(s-1)) =d(s-1)+1-p_a(X)$. Since $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1))=0$, one obtains $h^0(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(s-1))\geq h^0(\enm{\cal{O}}
_{\enm{\mathbb{P}}^n}(s-1)) =\binom{n+s-1}{n}$, and so: 
\[
p_a(X)\le d(s-1)+1-\binom{n+s-1}{n}.
\]
\end{remark}

\begin{question}\label{questiongeneralizedrangeA}
We pose the following questions:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] For which choices of $d, s, n$, does there exist $X\in \enm{\cal{B}} (n,s,d)$ (or even $X\in \enm{\cal{B}} (n,s,d)'$) such that $p_a(X) =d(s-1)+1-\binom{n+s-1}{n}$?
\item[(ii)] What is the maximal arithmetic genus of curves in $\enm{\cal{B}} (n,s,d)$ (or in $\enm{\cal{B}} (n,s,d)'$)?
\item[(iii)] For which $g_0$ and every $0\le g \le g_0$, does there exist $X\in \enm{\cal{B}} (n,s,d)$ (or $X\in \enm{\cal{B}} (n,s,d)'$) with such arithmetic genus? 
\end{enumerate}
\end{question}

\begin{remark}\label{numrangexq1true}

\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] $0 \le g \le d-n$, 

\item[(ii)] $(n+1)d \ge ng +n(n+1)$,

\item[(iii)] $(s-1)d \ge \binom{n+s-1}{n} +g-1$, and

\begin{proof}
Let $H\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^n$ be a linear subspace with $\dim H = n-m$. Take a linear subspace $E\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^n$ such that $\dim E =m-1$
and $E\cap H=\emptyset$. By \cite{hi, be2} (for the case $n=4$), \cite{be2} (for the case $n=5$) and \cite{be3} (for the case $n\ge 6$), there exists a smooth rational curve $Y\subset H$ such that 
\[
\deg (Y) =d_{n-m,s},\ \ h^0(H,\enm{\cal{I}} _{Y,H}(s-1)) =0,\ \mbox{and} \ \ h^0(H,\enm{\cal{I}} _{Y,H}(s)) = \binom{n+s-m}{n-m} -d_{n-m,s}.
\]

Let $W'$ be the cone with vertex $E$ and such a curve $Y\subset H$ as its base. Up to a projective transformation, the
projective variety depends only on $Y$, and not on the choice of a linear space $E$ such that $E\cap H = \emptyset$. 
Consider the setting described in Remark \ref{ccc0} with $e =d_{n-m,s}$. Note that $W'$ is projectively equivalent to the $(m+1)$-dimensional minimal degree variety $W$ featured in Remark \ref{ccc0}. Let $X\subset W'$ be an integral divisor such that $X\in |h+df|$, upon an identification $W\cong W'$. Since $d\geq (s-1)d_{n-m,s}+1$, by Remark \ref{ccc0}, $X$ is not contained in any hypersurface of degree $s-1$. 

If $X$ were a cone, either its vertex is contained in $E$ or is a point on $Y$. In the first case, upon identification with $W$, as in Remark \ref{ccc0}, let $X'=u^{*}X$ be the pullback of $X$ through $u$. The image of $h\cap u^{*}X$ under the morphism $u$ would be a codimension-one linear space in $u(h)\cong E$. However, this is impossible, as the degree of $u(h\cap X)$ is $d-d_{n-m,s}>1$. 
The second case is not possible either, because the pullback $X'$ would contain the divisor $h$. However, $X'$ is integral because $u$ is an isomorphism outside $h$, and $X'$ cannot coincide with $h$, as $X$ is a divisor of $W$. 
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}
Fix a general $C\in |\enm{\cal{O}} _X(s)|$. By Bertini's theorem, $C$ is a smooth and connected curve of degree $sd$. By the genus formula, $C$ has genus 
\[
g = 1 + (s^2d + \omega _X\cdot \enm{\cal{O}} _X(s))/2. 
\]
Multiplying by the section $C$ yields the exact sequence 
\begin{equation}\label{eqma1}
0 \to \enm{\cal{O}} _X\to \enm{\cal{O}} _X(s)\to \enm{\cal{O}} _C(s)\to 0.
\end{equation}

Thus $h^0(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(s)) \le h^0(\enm{\cal{O}} _C(s)) +1$, where equality holds if $h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X)=0$. \\
If $s^2d = \deg (\enm{\cal{O}} _C(s)) \le 2g-2$, then this divisor on $C$ is special and Clifford's theorem \cite[pp. 107--108]{acgh} gives 
\[
h^0(\enm{\cal{O}} _C(s)) \le 1 +s^2d/2. 
\]
Whence $h^0(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(s))\le 2 +s^2d/2$.

From now on, assume $s^2d\ge 2g-1$ (or equivalently, $\enm{\cal{O}} _C(s)$ is non-special). Again, by the genus formula, one has 
\[
\omega _X \cdot \enm{\cal{O}} _X(1) <0.
\] 
Note that Riemann-Roch gives $h^0(\enm{\cal{O}} _C(s)) =s^2d +1-g = \frac{1}{2}(s^2d -s\omega _X\cdot \enm{\cal{O}} _X(1))$.

Before we proceed, recall that a line bundle $\mathcal L$ on a projective variety $X$ of dimension $\ge 2$ is said to be \emph{nef} if $\mathcal L \cdot C\ge 0$, for every algebraic curve $C\subset X$. 
\begin{quote}
{\it Claim.} If $\omega _X \cdot \enm{\cal{O}} _X(1) <0$, then $\kappa (X)=-\infty$. \\
{\it Proof of the Claim.} Assume on the contrary that $\kappa (X)\ge 0$. Let $X'$ be the minimal model of $X$ and $\varphi: X\to X'$ be the corresponding morphism. Since $\kappa (X') =\kappa (X)\ge 0$, $\omega _{X'}$ is nef. We have $\omega _X \cong \varphi^\ast\omega _{X'} +E$, where $E$ is an effective divisor and $E = 0$ if and only if $X$ is minimal. Since $\varphi^\ast\omega _{X'}$ is nef and $\enm{\cal{O}}_X(1)$ is effective, we derive 
\[
( \varphi^\ast \omega _{X'} +E)\cdot \enm{\cal{O}} _X(1)\ge 0,
\]
which is a contradiction. 
\end{quote}
The {\it Claim} shows that the Kodaira dimension of $X$ is $\kappa (X) = -\infty$, and statement (i) is proven. 

We recall the Kawamata Rationality Theorem in the case of smooth surfaces. Let $X$ be a smooth projective surface such that $\omega _X$ is {\it not} nef. For each ample line bundle $\enm{\cal{L}}$ on $X$, the {\it nef-value} $\tau$ of $\enm{\cal{L}}$ with respect to $\omega_X$ is defined as 
\[
\tau(\enm{\cal{L}}) = \sup \lbrace t>0 \ | \  \enm{\cal{L}} +t\omega _X \mbox{ is nef} \rbrace, 
\]
where  $\enm{\cal{L}} +t\omega _X$ is viewed as a functional on the cone of curves depending on a parameter $t$. The aforementioned theorem states that the real number $\tau$ is rational, $\tau = u/v$, where $u$ is a positive integer and $v\in \{1,2,3\}$; see, e.g., \cite[Theorem 1.5.2]{bs}, \cite[Corollary 1-2-15]{matsuki}. Moreover, $\enm{\cal{L}} +\tau \omega_X$ is nef \cite[Lemma 1.5.5]{bs}, \cite[Theorem 1-2-14]{matsuki}. Thus
we have the following cases:

\begin{itemize}
\item $u=1$ and $v=3$. The cone of curves of $X$ has an {\it extremal ray} of {\it length} $3 =\dim X +1$; see \cite{matsuki} for these notions. This implies $X\cong \enm{\mathbb{P}}^2$ and $\enm{\cal{O}} _X(1)$ is the generator of $\mathrm{Pic}(X)$. Since $n\ge 4$, $X$ is embedded as described in the statement. 
\vspace{2mm}
\item $u=1$ and $v=2$. Since $\enm{\cal{L}}+\frac{1}{2}\omega _X$ is nef, so is the line bundle $2\enm{\cal{L}}+\omega _X$. In this case, there exists a curve $C\subset X$ such that $C\cdot (2\enm{\cal{L}}+\omega _X) =0$. By \cite[Theorem 1-4-8]{matsuki}, $X$ is a $\enm{\mathbb{P}}^1$-bundle over a smooth curve $D$, $\pi: X\to D$, and $\enm{\cal{L}}\cong\enm{\cal{O}} _X(1)$ has degree $1$ on each fiber $C$ of $\pi$. In such a case, $\omega _X(2)$ is nef and hence $\omega_X\cdot \enm{\cal{O}}_X(1) \geq -2$. This proves statement (ii). \\
\vspace{2mm}
\item $u\ge 2$ or $v=1$. Then $\omega _X^{\otimes 2}(3)$ is nef and therefore $\omega_X\cdot \enm{\cal{O}}_X(1)\geq -3/2$. In this case,
we obtain (iv). 
\end{itemize}
In conclusion, the discussion above yields $\omega_X\cdot \enm{\cal{O}}_X(1)\geq -3$ for all $X$, with equality if and only if $X\cong \enm{\mathbb{P}}^2$. This proves statement (iii).\end{proof}

\begin{remark}\label{ma2}
Let $n, s$ be integers as in the assumptions of Theorem \ref{ma1}, and let $k$ be an integer.  Assume $\binom{n+s}{n} \le 1+(s^2+3s)k^2/2$. From the ideal sheaf exact sequence and Theorem \ref{ma1} (iii), one has 
\[
h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s)) \ge 1+(s^2+3s)k^2/2 -\binom{n+s}{n},
\]
for any isomorphic projection $X\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^n$ of the degree $k$ Veronese embedding of $\enm{\mathbb{P}}^2$. Assuming the existence of such an $X$ with the additional property that the latter inequality is an equality, one obtains $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}}_X(s))=0$. Thus $d_{n,s+1,2} \le \deg(X) = k^2$. 
\end{remark}

\begin{proof}
The first part is statement (iii) of Theorem \ref{ma1}. By Proposition \ref{be1}, the general isomorphic linear projection of the degree $k$ Veronese surface has 
\[
h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(2)) =\max \left\{0,\binom{n+2}{2} -\binom{2k+2}{2}\right\}.
\] 
Thus the choice $k = n/2$ establishes the second statement. 
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}\label{w2}
Let $X\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^n$ be an integral and non-degenerate surface of sectional genus $g$ and degree $d$. Then $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _{X}(2)) \le \binom{n+1}{2} - 2d-1+g$.
\begin{proof}
Let $H\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^n$ be a general hyperplane. Consider the exact sequence
\begin{equation}\label{eqw1}
0 \longrightarrow \enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1)\longrightarrow \enm{\cal{I}} _X(s)\longrightarrow \enm{\cal{I}} _{X\cap H,H}(s)\longrightarrow 0.
\end{equation}
Since $H$ is general, $C = X\cap H$ is a smooth curve of degree $d$ and genus $g$. Hence, by Riemann-Roch, $h^0(\enm{\cal{O}}_C(2)) \geq 2d+1-g$. 
Thus 
\[
h^0(H,\enm{\cal{I}} _{X\cap H,H}(2)) \le \binom{n+1}{2} - 2d-1+g.
\] 
By (\ref{eqw1}) and $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(1)) =0$, the conclusion follows.
\end{proof}
\end{remark}


\begin{remark}\label{w3}
A complete classification of surfaces  of almost-minimal degree, i.e., all integral and non-degenerate surfaces $X\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^n$ such that $\deg (X) =n$ is known; see, e.g., \cite{hsv, park1}. Let $H\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^n$ be a general hyperplane. Since $C=X\cap H$ is a degree $n$ integral curve spanning $H$, there are two possibilities: either $C$ is arithmetically Cohen-Macaulay with $p_a(C) =1$ or $C$ is a smooth rational curve. In the latter case, $X$ may have only finitely many singular points. 

\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] $C$ is arithmetically Cohen-Macaulay with $p_a({C}) =1$. The surface $X$ is linearly normal of degree $\deg(X)\geq 2p_a(C)+1$. Note that this case may occur for all $n$: take a cone over a linearly normal elliptic curve $C\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^{n-1}$. 
\vspace{3mm}
\item[(ii)] $C$ is a smooth rational curve. Thus $h^1(H,\enm{\cal{I}} _{X\cap H,H}(1)) =1$, $h^1(H,\enm{\cal{I}} _{X\cap H,H}(2)) =0$, 
and so $h^0(H,\enm{\cal{I}} _{X\cap H,H}(2)) = \binom{n+1}{2} -2n-1$. It is clear that
\[
h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(1)) \le h^1(H,\enm{\cal{I}} _{X\cap H,H}(1)) =1.
\]
From (\ref{eqw1}), we derive $\binom{n+1}{2} -2n-2\le h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(2)) \le \binom{n+1}{2} -2n-1$. Now, if $X$ is smooth and $X\cap H$ is rational, then the classification of surfaces gives that $X$ is rational. Thus $h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X)=0$. A standard exact sequence gives $h^0(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(1)) =h^0(\enm{\cal{O}} _{X\cap H}(1)) +1=n+2$ and $h^0(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(2))= h^0(\enm{\cal{O}} _{X\cap H}(2)) +h^0(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(1)) = 3n+3$. Thus $h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(1)) =1$ and so $X$ is not linearly normal. Let $X'\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^{n+1}$ be a smooth surface such that $X$ is an isomorphic linear projection of $X'$ from some $p\in \enm{\mathbb{P}}^{n+1}$ with $p$ not contained in the secant variety of $X'$. Thus $\deg(X') = n$ and since $X'\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^{n+1}$, it is either a minimal degree surface scroll or (when $n=4$) the Veronese surface. In any case, one knows the minimal free resolution of $X'$, and it follows that $X'$ has property $K_2$, following Alzati and Russo \cite[Definition 3.1]{ar}.  By \cite[Theorem 3.2 or Corollary 3.3]{ar}, we have $h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(2))=0$. Hence $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(2)) =\binom{n+2}{2} -3n-3$.
\end{enumerate}

\end{remark}

\begin{proof}
Let 
\[
\delta =  \left\lceil \left(\binom{n+s-1}{n}-1\right)/(s-1)\right\rceil.
\]
We show that $d_{n,s} = \delta$. 

For any integer $d\ge n$, the set $H(d,0;n)$ of all smooth and non-degenerate degree $d$ rational curves $X\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^n$ has the structure of a smooth and integral algebraic variety, whose general point $X$ has {\it maximal rank}: hence $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(t)) =0$ for some $t\in \enm{\mathbb{N}}$ if and only if $d t+1\geq h^0(\enm{\cal{O}}_{\enm{\mathbb{P}}^n}(t))$, i.e., whenever it is possible for the restriction morphism to be injective; see \cite{hi, be3}. Thus a general $X\in H(d,0;n)$ satisfies
\[
h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1)) =0 \ \ \mbox{ if and only if } \ \ (s-1)d+1\ge \binom{n+s-1}{n}. 
\] 
This implies that $d_{n,s}\leq \delta$, as we have a (rational) integral curve of degree $\delta$. 

For the converse inequality, consider any integral curve $Y\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^n$ such that $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _Y(s-1)) =0$, and let $k = \deg (Y)$. Since $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _Y(s-1)) =0$, we have $h^0(\enm{\cal{O}} _Y(s-1)) \ge \binom{n+s-1}{n}$. Since $Y$ is an integral curve (of arbitrary arithmetic genus), elementary considerations give 
\[
h^0(L) \le \deg (L)+1,
\] 
for an arbitrary line bundle $L$ on $Y$. Thus 
\[
\deg(\enm{\cal{O}}_Y(s-1))+1 = (s-1)k+1 \ge h^0(\enm{\cal{O}}_Y(s-1))\geq \binom{n+s-1}{n}.
\]
Taking the minimum, the latter inequality implies $d_{n,s}\geq \delta$, which completes the proof. 
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}
Since $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1))=0$, Riemann-Roch shows that the statement is true if $h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(s-1)) =0$. Otherwise, assume $h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(s-1)) >0$. Since $h^0(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(s-1)) \ge \binom{n+s-1}{n}$, Clifford's theorem gives $(s-1)d_{n,s} \ge 2\binom{n+s-1}{n}-2$. By Proposition \ref{i1}, we have 
\[
(s-1)(d_{n,s} -1)+2 \le \binom{n+s-1}{n}.
\]
Altogether, they give $\binom{n+s-1}{n}\le s-1$, contradicting the assumption $s\ge 3$.  
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}\label{i3}
Fix an integer $g$ such that $0\le g \le  (s-1)d_{n,s}+1-\binom{n+s-1}{n}$. Again, as in the proof of Lemma \ref{i2}, Proposition \ref{i1} yields
\[
(s-1)(d_{n,s} -1)+2 \le \binom{n+s-1}{n},
\] 
and so $g\le s-2$. 
\vspace{3mm}

\begin{quote}
{\it Claim.} We have $s-2 \le d_{n,s}-n$.\\
{\it Proof of the Claim.} By contradiction, assume $d_{n,s} \le n+s-3$. By Proposition \ref{i1}, in order to obtain a contradiction, it is enough to show 
\[
(s-1)(n+s-3) +2 \le \binom{n+s-1}{n}.
\] 
Let $\varphi (n,s) = \binom{n+s-1}{n} - (s-1)(n+s-3)-2$. This function is non-negative in the desired range. Indeed, consider
\[
\varphi (3,s) = (s+2)(s+1)s/6 -s(s-1)-2.
\]
It is clear this is non-negative for all $s\ge 3$. Moreover: 
\[
\varphi (n+1,s) -\varphi (n,s) =\binom{n+s-2}{n} -s+1 \ge 0, \ \ \mbox{ for all } \ \  s\ge 3, 
\]
which leads to a contradiction. 
\end{quote}

By the {\it Claim} and \cite{be2, be3}, a general curve $X\in H(d_{n,s},g;n)'$ has maximal rank. Moreover, for each integer $g$ with $0\le
g\le  (s-1)d_{n,s}+1-\binom{n+s-1}{n}$, there exists a curve $X\in H(d_{n,s},g;n)$ such that $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1))=0$. Since $h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(1)) =0$, we
have $h^0(\omega_X(-1)) = 0$. The latter condition is equivalent to $h^0(\omega_X(-t))=0$ for all $t\geq 1$. 
Hence $h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(t)) =0$ for $t=s-1,s$. Moreover, we have: 
\[
h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1)) = (s-1)d_{n,s}+1-g -\binom{n+s-1}{n},
\]
\[
h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s)) = h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s)) +\binom{n+s}{n} -sd_{n,s}-1+g.
\] 
Now, choose $g_0 = (s-1)d_{n,s} + 1 -\binom{n+s-1}{n}$, so that $h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1)) =0$. 
Furthermore 
\[
h^2(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-2)) =h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(s-2)) =0,
\] 
where the right-most equality holds because $s\ge3$. By the well-known Castelnuovo-Mumford's Lemma, we derive 
\[h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(t)) =0 \mbox{ for all } t\ge s. \] 
Finally,
\[
h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s)) =\binom{n+s}{n} -sd_{n,s}-1+g_0 = \binom{n+s-1}{n-1}-d_{n,s}.
\]
\end{remark}

To summarize, in Remark \ref{i3}, we have shown the following: 

\begin{remark}\label{observation}
Setting $g_0 = (s-1)d_{n,s} + 1 -\binom{n+s-1}{n}$, We have: 
\[
d_{n,s} \ge n+g_0;
\]
additionally, a general curve $X\in H(d,g_0;n)'$ satisfies 
\[
h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1)) =0 \mbox{ and } h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s))=\binom{n+s-1}{n-1} -d_{n,s}.
\]
\end{remark}


\begin{question}\label{qw0}
Is it true that 
\[
\alpha (n,s) = \binom{n+s-1}{n-1} -d_{n,s}?
\] 
Keep the definition of $g_0$ from Remark \ref{observation}. Does equality hold if and only if $X$ is a general curve in $H(d_{n,s}, g_0; n)'$?
\end{question}

\begin{proof}
Fix a general hyperplane $H\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^n$. Note that $h^0(H,\enm{\cal{I}} _{X\cap H}(s)) =\binom{n+s-1}{n-1}-\deg (X)+h^1(H,\enm{\cal{I}} _{X\cap H}(s))$. Since $h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(t)) =h^2(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(t))$ for all $t\in \mathbb Z$, in order to conclude it is sufficient to use the long exact sequence in cohomology of the exact sequence
\begin{equation}\label{eqi01}
0\to \enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1)\to \enm{\cal{I}} _X(s)\to \enm{\cal{I}} _{X\cap H,H}(s)\to 0, 
\end{equation}
along with the assumption $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1)) =0$.
\end{proof}

Now we discuss the term appearing on the right-hand side of equality (\ref{eqi00+}). 

\begin{remark}\label{qw00}
In the setting of Lemma \ref{i00+}, as usual let $d = \deg (X)$ and $g = p_a(X)$. 
Since $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1)) =0$, by Riemann-Roch, we have 
\[
h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1)) = (s-1)d +1-g-\binom{n+s-1}{n}.
\] 
Define the numerical function $\psi (t) := h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(t-1)) -h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(t))$. For fixed integers $g$, $h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s))$ and $\psi(s)$, the right-hand side of (\ref{eqi00+}) is a strictly decreasing function in $d$.

Since $\deg (\enm{\cal{O}} _X(t)) =d+\deg (\enm{\cal{O}} _X(t-1))$, Serre duality and Riemann-Roch give 
\[
0\le \psi (t) \le d.
\]
Therefore a class of curves for which the term $h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(s-1)) -h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(s))$ is zero is realized when $h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(s-1)) =0$.

Moreover, note that the long exact sequence in cohomology of (\ref{eqi01}) yields
\[
h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s)) \le \binom{n+s-1}{n-1} -d,
\] 
whenever $h^1(H,\enm{\cal{I}} _{X\cap H,H}(s)) =0$. As in \cite[Chapter 3]{szp}, let $\chi$ denote the minimal non-negative integer such that $h^1(H,\enm{\cal{I}} _{X\cap H,H}(\chi +1)) =0$. As classically shown by Castelnuovo, using (\ref{eqi01}) one obtains $h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(t)) =0$ for all $t\ge \chi$ \cite[Theorem 1, p. 52]{szp}.
Furthermore, $h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(t)) \ge h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(t+1))$ for all $t\ge \chi$ \cite[Lemma 2, p. 53]{szp}, 
and $h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(t))> h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(t+1))$ whenever $t>\chi$ and $h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(t))\ne 0$.


\end{remark}

Note that the proof of Proposition \ref{i1} shows that a curve in $\mathcal A(n,s)$ of minimal degree $d_{n,s}$ can be chosen to be smooth (and rational). 
More generally, we wonder the following: 

\begin{question}\label{xq1}
Let $n\ge 3$, $s\ge 3$ and $d> d_{n,s}$. 
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] Is there an integral and non-degenerate curve $X\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^n$ such that $\deg (X)=d$, $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1)) =0$ and
$h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s))\ne 0$?
\item[(ii)] Can we choose such an $X$ to be smooth?
\end{enumerate}
\end{question}

\begin{remark}\label{x2}

\[

For $d, s\ge 3$, to  each pair $(d,s)$, we attach the set of degree $d$ curves in $\enm{\mathbb{P}}^3$ 
{\it not} contained in any surface of degree $<s$. Given $(d,s)$, Halphen's question asks in particular to determine the maximum genus of a curve associated to this pair. It is customary to divide the set of pairs $(d,s)$ into four regions: \\

{\bf Range $\emptyset$}: $d < (s^2+4s+6)/6 $. In this range, there is no integral and non-degenerate curve $X\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^3$ such that
$\deg (X)=d$ and $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1))=0$ \cite[Theorem 3.3]{h0}, \cite{hh}. 

\vspace{5mm}
{\bf Range A}: $(s^2+4s+6)/6 \le d < (s^2+4s+6)/3$. In this range, one finds curves with  
$h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(s-1)) =0$ and hence $h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(s))=0$. Thus if $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1))=0$ and $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s)) \ne 0$, by Riemann-Roch one has $(s-1)d+1-g
\ge \binom{s+2}{3}$ and $sd+1-g\le \binom{s+3}{3}$. Moreover, if $\lceil s(s+2)/4\rceil \le d <(s^2+4s+6)/3$, it is known such a curve exists for any such choice of $(d,s)$, along with curves reaching the maximal genera allowed; see, e.g., \cite{bbem, fl1,fl2}.  To fill in all 
$(d,s)$ such that $(s^2+4s+6)/6\le d < \lceil s(s+2)/4\rceil$ the same result (the existence of curves with $(d,s)$ and $g= (s-1)d+1- \binom{s+2}{3}$) is only known for $s$ large enough, i.e., $s \geq 10.5\times 10^5$, by the recent \cite[Theorem 1]{be6}. 

\vspace{5mm}
{\bf Range B}: $(s^2+4s+6)/3\le d < s(s-1)$. Hartshorne and Hirschowitz constructed, for any $(d, s)$ in this range, smooth space curves with very high genera and conjectured that they have the maximal genus for all curves associated to $(d,s)$ \cite{hh, ms}. 

\vspace{5mm}
{\bf Range C}: $d>s(s-1)$. One finds a smooth degree $d$ space curve $X$ such that
$\deg (X)=d$ and $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1))=0$; Gruson and Peskine classified all such curves $X$ of maximal genus \cite{gp1}: 
if $d\equiv 0\pmod{s}$, these curves are complete intersections of a surface of degree $s$ and a surface of degree $d/s$; in all other
cases $X$ is {\it linked} to a plane curve $C$ of degree $\deg(C) = s\lceil d/s\rceil -d$, by the complete intersection of a surface of degree $s$
and a surface of degree $\lceil d/s\rceil$. For $d\geq s^2$, we have $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s)) \le 2$ with equality if and only if $d=s^2$
and $X$ is the complete intersection of two surfaces of degree $s$.
\end{remark}


\begin{remark}\label{x3}

$X\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^3$ be any integral curve with $\deg (X)=d$, $h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(s-1)) =0$, $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1)) =0$, and $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s))
\ne 0$, i.e., by Riemann-Roch one has $(s-1)d+1-g\ge \binom{s+2}{3}$, and $sd+1-g\le \binom{s+3}{3}$, where $g = p_a(X)$ is the arithmetic genus
of $X$. All curves constructed in \cite{bbem, be6, bef, fl1, fl2} have $h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1)) = h^2(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1)) =0$ and hence $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s)) =\binom{s+2}{2} - d$. We generalize {\bf Range A} to curves embedded in $\enm{\mathbb{P}}^n$ for any $n\geq 3$. For all integers $n\geq 3$, $s\ge 2$ and $d\ge d_{n,s}$, let $\enm{\cal{B}} (n,s,d)$ (resp. $\enm{\cal{B}} (n,s,d)'$) denote the set of all smooth and connected (resp. integral) $X\in \enm{\cal{A}} (n,s)$ such that $\deg (X)=d$ and $h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(s-1)) = 0$.

\begin{definition}
Curves in $\enm{\cal{B}} (n,s,d)$ are said to be in the {\it generalized} {\bf Range A}.
\end{definition}

\begin{remark}
Let $X\in \enm{\cal{B}} (n,s,d)'$. Since $h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(s-1))  =0$,

_{\enm{\mathbb{P}}^n}(s-1)) =\binom{n+s-1}{n}$, and so: 
\[
p_a(X)\le d(s-1)+1-\binom{n+s-1}{n}.
\]
\end{remark}

\begin{question}\label{questiongeneralizedrangeA}

\item[(iii)] For which $g_0$ and every $0\le g \le g_0$, does there exist $X\in \enm{\cal{B}} (n,s,d)$ (or $X\in \enm{\cal{B}} (n,s,d)'$) with such arithmetic genus?

\begin{remark}\label{numrangexq1true}
Fix integers $n, d, g, s$ such that $n\ge 3$, $s\ge 3$, with

\item[(i)] $0 \le g \le d-n$, 

\item[(ii)] $(n+1)d \ge ng +n(n+1)$,

\item[(iii)] $(s-1)d \ge \binom{n+s-1}{n} +g-1$, and

\item[(iv)] $sd \le \binom{n+s-1}{n}+g-2$.

\[

We recall the Kawamata Rationality Theorem in the case of smooth surfaces. Let $X$ be a smooth projective surface such that $\omega _X$ is {\it not} nef. For each ample line bundle $\enm{\cal{L}}$ on $X$, the {\it nef-value} $\tau$ of $\enm{\cal{L}}$ with respect to $\omega_X$ is defined as

\begin{remark}\label{w2}
Let $X\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^n$ be an integral and non-degenerate surface of sectional genus $g$ and degree $d$. Then $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _{X}(2)) \le \binom{n+1}{2} - 2d-1+g$.
\begin{proof}
Let $H\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^n$ be a general hyperplane. Consider the exact sequence
\begin{equation}\label{eqw1}

\end{equation}
Since $H$ is general, $C = X\cap H$ is a smooth curve of degree $d$ and genus $g$. Hence, by Riemann-Roch, $h^0(\enm{\cal{O}}_C(2)) \geq 2d+1-g$. 
Thus 
\[
h^0(H,\enm{\cal{I}} _{X\cap H,H}(2)) \le \binom{n+1}{2} - 2d-1+g.
\] 
By (\ref{eqw1}) and $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(1)) =0$, the conclusion follows.

\begin{remark}\label{w3}
A complete classification of surfaces  of almost-minimal degree, i.e., all integral and non-degenerate surfaces $X\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^n$ such that $\deg (X) =n$ is known; see, e.g., \cite{hsv, park1}. Let $H\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^n$ be a general hyperplane. Since $C=X\cap H$ is a degree $n$ integral curve spanning $H$, there are two possibilities: either $C$ is arithmetically Cohen-Macaulay with $p_a(C) =1$ or $C$ is a smooth rational curve. In the latter case, $X$ may have only finitely many singular points. 

\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] $C$ is arithmetically Cohen-Macaulay with $p_a({C}) =1$. The surface $X$ is linearly normal of degree $\deg(X)\geq 2p_a(C)+1$. Note that this case may occur for all $n$: take a cone over a linearly normal elliptic curve $C\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^{n-1}$.

\item[(ii)] $C$ is a smooth rational curve. Thus $h^1(H,\enm{\cal{I}} _{X\cap H,H}(1)) =1$, $h^1(H,\enm{\cal{I}} _{X\cap H,H}(2)) =0$,

\[

\]

Thus $\deg(X') = n$ and since $X'\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^{n+1}$, it is either a minimal degree surface scroll or (when $n=4$) the Veronese surface. In any case, one knows the minimal free resolution of $X'$, and it follows that $X'$ has property $K_2$, following Alzati and Russo \cite[Definition 3.1]{ar}.  By \cite[Theorem 3.2 or Corollary 3.3]{ar}, we have $h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(2))=0$. Hence $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(2)) =\binom{n+2}{2} -3n-3$.
\end{enumerate}

\end{remark}

\label{i3}
Fix an integer $g$ such that $0\le g \le  (s-1)d_{n,s}+1-\binom{n+s-1}{n}$. Again, as in the proof of Lemma \ref{i2}, Proposition \ref{i1} yields
\[
(s-1)(d_{n,s} -1)+2 \le \binom{n+s-1}{n},
\] 
and so $g\le s-2$. 
\vspace{3mm}

\begin{quote}
{\it Claim.} We have $s-2 \le d_{n,s}-n$.\\
{\it Proof of the Claim.} By contradiction, assume $d_{n,s} \le n+s-3$. By Proposition \ref{i1}, in order to obtain a contradiction, it is enough to show 
\[
(s-1)(n+s-3) +2 \le \binom{n+s-1}{n}.
\] 
Let $\varphi (n,s) = \binom{n+s-1}{n} - (s-1)(n+s-3)-2$. This function is non-negative in the desired range. Indeed, consider
\[
\varphi (3,s) = (s+2)(s+1)s/6 -s(s-1)-2.
\]
It is clear this is non-negative for all $s\ge 3$. Moreover: 
\[
\varphi (n+1,s) -\varphi (n,s) =\binom{n+s-2}{n} -s+1 \ge 0, \ \ \mbox{ for all } \ \  s\ge 3, 
\]
which leads to a contradiction. 
\end{quote}

By the {\it Claim} and \cite{be2, be3}, a general curve $X\in H(d_{n,s},g;n)'$ has maximal rank. Moreover, for each integer $g$ with $0\le
g\le  (s-1)d_{n,s}+1-\binom{n+s-1}{n}$, there exists a curve $X\in H(d_{n,s},g;n)$ such that $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1))=0$. Since $h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(1)) =0$, we
have $h^0(\omega_X(-1)) = 0$. The latter condition is equivalent to $h^0(\omega_X(-t))=0$ for all $t\geq 1$. 
Hence $h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(t)) =0$ for $t=s-1,s$. Moreover, we have: 
\[
h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1)) = (s-1)d_{n,s}+1-g -\binom{n+s-1}{n},
\]
\[
h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s)) = h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s)) +\binom{n+s}{n} -sd_{n,s}-1+g.
\] 
Now, choose $g_0 = (s-1)d_{n,s} + 1 -\binom{n+s-1}{n}$, so that $h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1)) =0$. 
Furthermore 
\[
h^2(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-2)) =h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(s-2)) =0,
\] 
where the right-most equality holds because $s\ge3$. By the well-known Castelnuovo-Mumford's Lemma, we derive 
\[h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(t)) =0 \mbox{ for all } t\ge s. \] 
Finally,
\[
h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s)) =\binom{n+s}{n} -sd_{n,s}-1+g_0 = \binom{n+s-1}{n-1}-d_{n,s}.
\]

\label{qw00}
In the setting of Lemma \ref{i00+}, as usual let $d = \deg (X)$ and $g = p_a(X)$. 
Since $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1)) =0$, by Riemann-Roch, we have 
\[
h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1)) = (s-1)d +1-g-\binom{n+s-1}{n}.
\] 
Define the numerical function $\psi (t) := h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(t-1)) -h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(t))$. For fixed integers $g$, $h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s))$ and $\psi(s)$, the right-hand side of (\ref{eqi00+}) is a strictly decreasing function in $d$.

Since $\deg (\enm{\cal{O}} _X(t)) =d+\deg (\enm{\cal{O}} _X(t-1))$, Serre duality and Riemann-Roch give 
\[
0\le \psi (t) \le d.
\]
Therefore a class of curves for which the term $h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(s-1)) -h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(s))$ is zero is realized when $h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(s-1)) =0$.

Moreover, note that the long exact sequence in cohomology of (\ref{eqi01}) yields
\[
h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s)) \le \binom{n+s-1}{n-1} -d,
\] 
whenever $h^1(H,\enm{\cal{I}} _{X\cap H,H}(s)) =0$. As in \cite[Chapter 3]{szp}, let $\chi$ denote the minimal non-negative integer such that $h^1(H,\enm{\cal{I}} _{X\cap H,H}(\chi +1)) =0$. As classically shown by Castelnuovo, using (\ref{eqi01}) one obtains $h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(t)) =0$ for all $t\ge \chi$ \cite[Theorem 1, p. 52]{szp}.
Furthermore, $h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(t)) \ge h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(t+1))$ for all $t\ge \chi$ \cite[Lemma 2, p. 53]{szp}, 
and $h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(t))> h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(t+1))$ whenever $t>\chi$ and $h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(t))\ne 0$.

\label{x2}
Recall that, by Proposition \ref{i1}, 
\[
d_{3,s} = \left\lceil \left(\binom{s+2}{3}-1\right)/(s-1)\right\rceil.
\]  
For $d, s\ge 3$, to  each pair $(d,s)$, we attach the set of degree $d$ curves in $\enm{\mathbb{P}}^3$ 
{\it not} contained in any surface of degree $<s$. Given $(d,s)$, Halphen's question asks in particular to determine the maximum genus of a curve associated to this pair. It is customary to divide the set of pairs $(d,s)$ into four regions: \\

{\bf Range $\emptyset$}: $d < (s^2+4s+6)/6 $. In this range, there is no integral and non-degenerate curve $X\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^3$ such that
$\deg (X)=d$ and $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1))=0$ \cite[Theorem 3.3]{h0}, \cite{hh}.

\label{numrangexq1true}
Fix integers $n, d, g, s$ such that $n\ge 3$, $s\ge 3$, with 
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] $0 \le g \le d-n$, 

\item[(ii)] $(n+1)d \ge ng +n(n+1)$,

\item[(iii)] $(s-1)d \ge \binom{n+s-1}{n} +g-1$, and

\item[(iv)] $sd \le \binom{n+s-1}{n}+g-2$.
\end{enumerate}
By results shown in \cite{be2, be4, be5}, there exists a smooth, connected, and non-degenerate {\it maximal rank} 
curve $X\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^n$ with $\deg (X) = d$, arithmetic genus $p_a(X)=g$, and $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s)) =\binom{n+s}{n} -sd+g-1$. Hence, setting the arithmetic genus to be the maximal in this range, i.e., $g=d-n$, (i) and (ii) in Question \ref{xq1} have a positive answer, whenever
\[
h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s))>0 \Longleftrightarrow (s-1)d < \binom{n+s}{n} -n-1.
\]
Note that inequality (iii) implies $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1)) = 0$, because $X$ has maximal rank.

\[

\]

\begin{quote}
{\it Claim.} We have $s-2 \le d_{n,s}-n$.\\
{\it Proof of the Claim.} By contradiction, assume $d_{n,s} \le n+s-3$. By Proposition \ref{i1}, in order to obtain a contradiction, it is enough to show 
\[
(s-1)(n+s-3) +2 \le \binom{n+s-1}{n}.
\] 
Let $\varphi (n,s) = \binom{n+s-1}{n} - (s-1)(n+s-3)-2$. This function is non-negative in the desired range. Indeed, consider
\[
\varphi (3,s) = (s+2)(s+1)s/6 -s(s-1)-2.
\]
It is clear this is non-negative for all $s\ge 3$. Moreover: 
\[
\varphi (n+1,s) -\varphi (n,s) =\binom{n+s-2}{n} -s+1 \ge 0, \ \ \mbox{ for all } \ \  s\ge 3, 
\]
which leads to a contradiction. 
\end{quote}

By the {\it Claim} and \cite{be2, be3}, a general curve $X\in H(d_{n,s},g;n)'$ has maximal rank. Moreover, for each integer $g$ with $0\le

Hence $h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(t)) =0$ for $t=s-1,s$. Moreover, we have: 
\[

\]
\[
h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s)) = h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s)) +\binom{n+s}{n} -sd_{n,s}-1+g.
\] 
Now, choose $g_0 = (s-1)d_{n,s} + 1 -\binom{n+s-1}{n}$, so that $h^1(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1)) =0$. 
Furthermore 
\[
h^2(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-2)) =h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(s-2)) =0,

\[

Recall that, by Proposition \ref{i1}, 
\[

\]  
For $d, s\ge 3$, to  each pair $(d,s)$, we attach the set of degree $d$ curves in $\enm{\mathbb{P}}^3$ 
{\it not} contained in any surface of degree $<s$. Given $(d,s)$, Halphen's question asks in particular to determine the maximum genus of a curve associated to this pair. It is customary to divide the set of pairs $(d,s)$ into four regions: \\

{\bf Range $\emptyset$}: $d < (s^2+4s+6)/6 $. In this range, there is no integral and non-degenerate curve $X\subset \enm{\mathbb{P}}^3$ such that
$\deg (X)=d$ and $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1))=0$ \cite[Theorem 3.3]{h0}, \cite{hh}. 

\vspace{5mm}
{\bf Range A}: $(s^2+4s+6)/6 \le d < (s^2+4s+6)/3$. In this range, one finds curves with  
$h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(s-1)) =0$ and hence $h^1(\enm{\cal{O}} _X(s))=0$. Thus if $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1))=0$ and $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s)) \ne 0$, by Riemann-Roch one has $(s-1)d+1-g
\ge \binom{s+2}{3}$ and $sd+1-g\le \binom{s+3}{3}$. Moreover, if $\lceil s(s+2)/4\rceil \le d <(s^2+4s+6)/3$, it is known such a curve exists for any such choice of $(d,s)$, along with curves reaching the maximal genera allowed; see, e.g., \cite{bbem, fl1,fl2}.  To fill in all 
$(d,s)$ such that $(s^2+4s+6)/6\le d < \lceil s(s+2)/4\rceil$ the same result (the existence of curves with $(d,s)$ and $g= (s-1)d+1- \binom{s+2}{3}$) is only known for $s$ large enough, i.e., $s \geq 10.5\times 10^5$, by the recent \cite[Theorem 1]{be6}. 

\vspace{5mm}
{\bf Range B}: $(s^2+4s+6)/3\le d < s(s-1)$. Hartshorne and Hirschowitz constructed, for any $(d, s)$ in this range, smooth space curves with very high genera and conjectured that they have the maximal genus for all curves associated to $(d,s)$ \cite{hh, ms}.

$\deg (X)=d$ and $h^0(\enm{\cal{I}} _X(s-1))=0$; Gruson and Peskine classified all such curves $X$ of maximal genus \cite{gp1}:

\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] $0 \le g \le d-n$, 

\item[(ii)] $(n+1)d \ge ng +n(n+1)$,

\item[(iii)] $(s-1)d \ge \binom{n+s-1}{n} +g-1$, and

\item[(iv)] $sd \le \binom{n+s-1}{n}+g-2$.

\]
